# Apple mode

Remora's explicit `apple` VNC mode implements the encrypted Apple RFB 003.889 profile. Standard mode remains the default. Apple mode logs in only with security type 36, Apple's SRP login, which proves the Mac's identity. [Login](#login) describes it. The mode also requires an extended shared ServerInit without session selection, and 32-bit RGB888 pixels. It advertises MVS encoding 1011, encryption pseudo-encoding 1103, Raw, DesktopSize, DisplayInfo and DisplayInfo2. DisplayInfo2 and DesktopSize may change framebuffer geometry. Unsupported profiles and invalid geometry end the attempt. There is no alternate authentication retry, virtual display, media, HEVC or dynamic resizing. The only reconnection is the same-profile transport recovery described under Connection reliability.

`mvs.c` and `mvs.h` derive from the v3 C port of [noVNC-ARD](https://github.com/peetinc/noVNC-ARD/tree/d699293635083c9e0c30c8f9480993865653772a/ard/decoders), revision `d699293635083c9e0c30c8f9480993865653772a`. The port covers full, partial, cache, match and quantization updates. Where the JavaScript and Screen Sharing's own decoder differ, the port follows Screen Sharing, as the next paragraphs describe. Remora adds per-pixel initialization masks to tile descriptors, stops partial updates and match copies that read uninitialized pixels, and resets picture descriptors at display acknowledgements. Raw writes establish pixel coverage without creating or changing MVS differential descriptors. The stream cache and quantizers survive picture resets. The originals had SHA-256 `7efd6151967b4bb1313f8f849cbd284663a5554542c8e459e144d0a470cd87fd` (C) and `2da0cf4349d12f2ed8289e399a230c011a7b609ed7299d3bec33f7c4e6f08c45` (header). The MPL-2.0 license is in `../licenses/Apple-MVS-MPL-2.0.txt`. The IDCT attribution and IJG notices are retained. New adapter code is GPL-3.0-or-later.

`mvs.c` decodes as Screen Sharing's own decoder does, and an oracle test checks that. `../tests/apple_oracle.c` loads `/System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/ScreenSharing.framework/Versions/A/ScreenSharing` into the test process. It calls the framework's unexported functions `_RFBInitializeConnectionRef`, `_RFBDefineCallback`, `_RFBSetLocalBitmap`, `_NetBufferAddData`, `_DecodeMVSUpdate`, `_jpeg_idct_islow` and `_Cache_Dispose` at addresses it reads from the image's symbol table. Nothing is copied out of the framework. Every stream of `../tests/test_mvs.c` then goes to both decoders. The two must succeed or fail together, and their pictures must be equal pixel for pixel after every update that both decode to its end.

On macOS 27.0.1 (26A434), arm64e, framework UUID `EC0B2C20-F816-3FCE-822D-F9403C09EB50`, the two agree on all of it. That is 300,000 transform blocks, with coefficients over the whole 16-bit range and quantizers from 0 to 255, and 246,488 updates, 239,290 of them with the pictures compared. The updates are the reference vectors, 600 full updates whose coefficients are as large as the codes carry, 65,000 cache writes with loads of slots 0, 1, 64999, 65000, 65001 and 65535, the golden and refinement sequences, the codes Screen Sharing stops at, and 200,000 fuzz cases. Eight more runs with other generator seeds agreed as well. On 2026-11-22 the same oracle also ran on macOS 26.6.2 (25G83), framework UUID `CFAE26CC-B46F-3629-9461-F5540C0E8D3D`, on the M3 Pro, with the same hashes and no differences.

The transform is libjpeg's `jpeg_idct_islow` in 32-bit arithmetic that wraps, with its shortcut for a column whose AC coefficients are all zero. Dequantized coefficients reach the wrapping range in valid streams: 16-bit coefficients times quantizers up to 255. Cache writes use slots 1 through 64999 and wrap to 1. A load of slot 0, of a slot above 65000 or of a slot beyond the number of writes draws nothing, and decoding continues. Slot 65000 is never written. Once 65000 entries were written a load of it draws an entry of zeros, which Screen Sharing reads from just past its 6,435,000-byte cache allocation. Remora allocates that slot.

Screen Sharing rejects, and Remora fails on: a full update whose DC value has a Rice prefix of more than 38 ones, whose AC value at positions 1 to 5 has one of more than 32, or whose long run of zeros reaches position 64; a wrong header or body marker; a body offset past the end; an unknown update type; and a quantization update that is not 129 bytes. Screen Sharing reads on, and so does Remora, in these cases. An AC value at positions 6 to 63 with a prefix of more than 18 ones ends its block 20 bits into the prefix; the tile is drawn from the coefficients read so far and keeps its old descriptor. A repeat tile with no DCT tile before it in the update is a tile of zeros. In a partial update a luma value in the DC code with a prefix of more than 38 ones is 0 after 40 bits, sixteen ones in place of a Huffman code end the block after 17 bits, and the three bytes after the last tile may be anything. The body of a full update may start anywhere in it, and its tile types may run on into the body. A tile's descriptor outlives tiles of other types drawn over it, so a later partial update refines the older DCT tile.

Three differences remain, and the oracle does not compare what they touch. First, Remora fails at the end of the payload, where Screen Sharing reads up to 500 bytes past it in a buffer it never cleared. Second, Remora stops a partial update or a copy that reads pixels nothing initialized, where Screen Sharing reads its bitmap as it is. The adapter then leaves the rest of that rectangle and requests the whole screen with a full, non-incremental FramebufferUpdateRequest. The session continues. Screen Sharing's only check of that kind returns -300 for a partial update that arrives before any full or quantization update. Third, Screen Sharing fills some tiles from memory outside the picture, which Remora leaves, or copies as far as the framebuffer goes. A tile the rect clips, with a copy that has no source, a match that has no reference or a cache slot that cannot be loaded, gets whatever Screen Sharing's 8x8 scratch tile on the stack holds. A copy whose source the framebuffer's right edge cuts short gets the pixels that follow in Screen Sharing's bitmap: with rows of 4 x width bytes, the first pixels of the next row. The decoder counts these tiles in `mvs_stats.unspecified`, and the oracle skips the picture of an update that has one. The adapter's whole-tile rects meet them only at a framebuffer edge that is not a multiple of 8.

The oracle compares decoders. It does not show what `screensharingd` encodes. Real-host validation is limited to the LAN measurements and editing workload below. An earlier controlled comparison with Apple's viewer covered only F0 and F1; its rejected F2 image was deleted and F3-F6 were not evaluated.

`apple.c` owns the private profile state. It parses bounded control bodies, limits compressed rectangles to the smaller of 64 MiB and `4 * rectangle area + 65536`, and accepts only aligned, framebuffer-contained MVS rectangles. The existing renderer limits remain 16384 pixels per axis and 67,108,864 pixels total. Any other malformed rectangle ends the session. There is no recovery using a partially consumed payload or a decoder that has failed.

Whole updates commit only after all rectangles validate. The adapter accumulates one bounding box from the decoder's existing written-tile callbacks and Raw rectangles, then publishes it once at the end of the message. DCT writes, cache loads and match copies contribute only their destination pixels, clipped at the framebuffer edge. Skipped tiles, skipped matches, loads of unusable cache slots and quantization updates add no damage. A full MVS update contributes its actual written region. Full updates may initialize separate displays in separate messages, with unused space between them. A partial update requires initialized pixels only in its own region, and DCT deltas also require valid coefficient descriptors. The session bridge publishes the first selected picture only after all selected pixels are initialized. It reports that selected geometry before delivering the picture, then marks the selection ready. One bounding box uses constant storage and preserves the existing single-rectangle renderer path. Distant writes can include unchanged pixels between them. No callback exposes an incomplete message, even if the decoder wrote pixels before detecting its error.

The adapter sends shared ClientInit `0x81` and control SetMode 1 before the initial full FramebufferUpdateRequest. It then enables full-region, zero-interval AutoFBUpdate (`0x09`) before waiting for a baseline. While visible and awaiting a complete baseline, the worker retries a full, non-incremental request once per second between messages. Controls and incomplete coverage do not reset that retry interval. A partial MVS frame over uninitialized pixels triggers one more full request, as described above. It sends no automatic type-3 request per pushed update. Hidden demand pauses retries and sends AutoFBUpdate interval `0xffffffff`; resume sends interval 0 and preserves the existing immediate full-refresh request. Both subscription messages use header flags 1. Repeated demand does not generate refreshes. Closing the transport ends the subscription.

These startup and pause records follow the arm64e ScreenSharing framework and AppleVNCServer installed with macOS 27.0.1 (26A434). ScreenSharing's `stRequestUpdates` sends `RFBCheckForUpdate(ref, 1, NULL)` at `0x1cc068044`, then calls `stSetFrameUpdateInterval` at `0x1cc068214` before receiving a frame. `stSetFrameUpdateInterval` passes AutoFBUpdate flags 1 and maps a negative interval to `0xffffffff` at `0x1cc0daf18`. AppleVNCServer's `HandleAutoFrameBufferUpdateMessage` at `0x10001708c` enables automatic updates exactly when the interval differs from `0xffffffff`. SetMode 0 observes, SetMode 1 controls, and SetMode 2 inhibits local physical input when the server permits it. SetMode does not select a frame rate; Remora uses SetMode 1.

Server messages ARDAck (`0x04`), NOP (`0x07`) and StateChange (`0x14`) are handled in this profile. DisplayInfo2 (`0x51`) is also handled on standard RFB connections to Macs. Legacy ServerCutText bodies in Apple mode are discarded in chunks of at most 4096 bytes, with a 1 MiB body limit. Unknown messages and unsupported rectangle encodings fail closed.

Apple mode shares plain text in both directions through the native pasteboard protocol. The clear prelude sends numeric ViewerInfo, control SetMode and AutoPasteboard start in that order. A pasteboard change marks the session's clipboard pending, so older text is not served, and triggers a full-data request with a viewer-generated ID. The adapter validates the complete archive before publishing the first `public.utf8-plain-text` flavor within 1 MiB from the latest request. It accepts finished and sync-flushed zlib streams. Archives up to 8 MiB in both declared sizes are inflated, which leaves room for rich companion flavors within a fixed memory budget. Larger archives, such as a copied image, are drained in 4 KiB chunks without inflating and report no text; the session continues. Declared sizes above Apple's 100 MiB server limit, and malformed archives, end the session with native error 17. A pasteboard change announced while the client waits for the encryption key is fetched right after activation. Invalid UTF-8 reports a failed clipboard transfer. Outbound text uses one UTF-8 flavor. An empty string sends a zero-flavor item to clear the remote pasteboard. [Prelude and layout](https://github.com/andrewtheguy/remotex/blob/a549005379b0ed4e57c8119c3e6848901dcc8e9f/src/vnc_apple.rs#L271-L301), [Pasteboard framing and clear operation](https://github.com/andrewtheguy/remotex/blob/a549005379b0ed4e57c8119c3e6848901dcc8e9f/src/vnc_apple_clipboard.rs).

After SetMode, the client sends SetEncryption commands 1 and 2 together. This ordering keeps all application writes, including SetPixelFormat and SetEncodings, behind the same activation point. The client accepts a clear Bell, status, acknowledgement, NOP or empty update while waiting for a single-rectangle update with encoding 1103 and generation 1. It applies the existing read deadline to the entire exchange. OpenSSL decrypts the two 16-byte blocks with AES-128-ECB under the first 16 bytes of SHA-256 of the login's SRP session key. These blocks supply the content key and initial IV. The client then erases the wrapping key. [Measured handshake and receive boundary](https://github.com/andrewtheguy/remotex/blob/a549005379b0ed4e57c8119c3e6848901dcc8e9f/src/vnc.rs#L3400-L3422)

The login proves the Mac's identity to the client. Only a server that holds the account's SRP verifier can compute the proof M2, and the client checks M2 before it sends ClientInit. The wrapping key comes from the same SRP secret, so a machine that relays the login cannot unwrap the record keys, read the session or forge its records. A machine that impersonates the Mac receives the account name, which travels in clear, and the client's proof M1. M1 tells it whether the one password guess it built into its challenge was right. It cannot test more guesses without another connection attempt from the user. Two limits remain, and neither exposes the password. First, the messages between the SecurityResult and the first record are clear and carry no integrity check, so a machine in the path can change them. That can end the attempt. It cannot yield the record keys: a changed key rectangle makes the first record fail its digest check. Second, SRP authenticates the login and not the TCP connection. A machine in the path can relay a login and then use the Mac's end of that connection itself, if the Mac serves a session without encryption after a type 36 login. Whether macOS does was not determined.

LibVNCClient reads and writes all subsequent RFB bytes through AES-128-CBC records. Each direction starts at sequence zero and keeps its own CBC chain. The reader consumes prefetched ciphertext from the same socket buffer as the clear handshake. It checks the ciphertext length, SHA-1 digest over the sequence and padded body, and declared body length before releasing any bytes from the record. A message can cross records, and one record can carry multiple messages. The client ends the attempt on encryption refusal, an invalid record or a subsequent key change. Key events (type 4) and pointer events (type 5) use ordinary RFB framing inside the records. [Record format](https://github.com/andrewtheguy/remotex/blob/a549005379b0ed4e57c8119c3e6848901dcc8e9f/src/vnc_record.rs#L79-L175) and [noVNC-ARD input handling](https://github.com/peetinc/noVNC-ARD/blob/d699293635083c9e0c30c8f9480993865653772a/ard/ard-patch.js#L1895-L1930)

Option maps to Meta, legacy character keysyms above Latin-1 map to Unicode, and right/middle button bits swap at the Apple wire boundary. Source ownership stays in the existing input worker. Discrete scrolling follows ard-rs revision `7ff47199541c364cbba16e29c4410e39898ece0e`, `crates/ard-core/src/protocol.rs:917` and `crates/ard-viewer/src/session_runtime.rs:2058`. Positive native horizontal deltas correspond to RFB left (0x20); Remora right (0x40) becomes negative. Discrete scrolling uses the source-defined type `0x17`, subtype 11 record with line, 16.16 and point deltas, the event position, and the existing held-button mask. A local system arrow is explicitly emitted; unsupported remote cursor-shape encodings are not advertised.

`../patches/libvncclient-apple.patch` connects this module to the pinned LibVNCClient. It adds Apple display metadata to standard-mode parsing and refuses generic reported multi-display layouts without a selection protocol. In Apple mode it selects security type 36 whatever else the server offers. Standard-mode selection is unchanged. `../build-vnc.sh` compiles this decoder in the Release engine with `-O3`, using the existing OpenSSL archive. `mise run test:mvs` runs `../tests/test-apple-mvs.sh`: the owned vectors, the cases at Screen Sharing's limits, hashes over 300,000 transform blocks and over 600 full updates with large coefficients, a golden hash over generated update sequences, another over 300 valid pairs of a full update and the partial update that refines it, and bounded fuzz cases, under ASan/UBSan. The golden and refinement hashes cover every update's result, statistics, written rectangles and pixels, so a faster decoder must reproduce the current output bit for bit. The script then builds the same tests without sanitizers and runs them as the oracle described above. The oracle prints the framework's UUID and the macOS build. Where it cannot call the framework it prints the reason and skips: the framework does not load, lacks a symbol, lays out its session differently, or crashes a probe process. On the two framework builds it was verified on, UUIDs `EC0B2C20-F816-3FCE-822D-F9403C09EB50` and `CFAE26CC-B46F-3629-9461-F5540C0E8D3D`, any of these fails the test instead. When the image cannot be read at all, macOS builds 26A434 and 25G83 on arm64 stand in for those UUIDs. `../tests/test-apple-mvs.sh bench` times generated partial updates of a 3024x1964 screen with the Release flags and no sanitizers. `python3 Vendor/tests/test-apple-session.py` drives the sanitized login, adapter and decoder through the public native API with the loopback peer, whose SRP server is an independent Python implementation, and once more with `../tests/srp_oracle.py`, whose SRP arithmetic is corecrypto's. Swift public-session tests exercise the same wire framing and independent CommonCrypto record encryption and decryption. None of these tests establish real-host usability.

## Login

On 2026-11-22 a MacBook Pro M3 Pro running macOS 26.6.2 (25G83) offered security types `[30, 33, 36, 2, 35]`, to an `RFB 003.889` client and to an `RFB 003.008` client alike. Types 30, 33 and 36 take an account name and a password. Apple mode selects type 36 whatever else is offered. It never selects another type, and no setting allows one. When the offer lacks type 36 the client sends no selection and no credentials, and the attempt ends with native error 18. macOS 10.15.6 already offered types 30, 33, 36 and 35 ([Apple developer forum thread 654421](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/654421)), so an offer without type 36 comes from an older Mac, from a Mac that has SRP turned off, or from a machine that strips the type to force a weaker login.

Type 30 is the Diffie-Hellman login that standard mode uses with Macs. The server sends a generator, a prime and its public value. The client answers with its public value and a 128-byte block that holds the account name and the password, under AES-128-ECB with the MD5 digest of the shared secret. Nothing authenticates the server's values. A machine that impersonates the Mac completes the exchange and decrypts the block.

Type 36 is SRP-6a. It is Apple's port of the SRP mechanism of Cyrus SASL to corecrypto's `ccsrp`. The published form is `cyrus_sasl/plugins/srp.c` in [passwordserver_sasl](https://github.com/apple-oss-distributions/passwordserver_sasl) at tag `passwordserver_sasl-215`. AppleVNCServer carries the path `Sources/RemoteDesktop/common/srp.m`, the verifier name `SRP-RFC5054-4096-SHA512-PBKDF2`, and imports of `ccsrp_ctx_init`, `ccsrp_server_generate_public_key`, `ccsrp_server_compute_session` and `ccsrp_server_verify_session`. The group is the 4096-bit group of RFC 5054 with generator 5. The hash is SHA-512.

Every SRP message is `[BE32 length][BE32 length - 4][fields]`. A number is a BE16 length and big-endian bytes without leading zeros. An octet string is a one-byte length and bytes. A text is a BE16 length and UTF-8 bytes. The exchange has four messages:

1. The client sends the byte `0x24`, then a message with an empty text, the account name as text, an empty text and an empty octet string. The byte and the message must arrive together. AppleVNCServer parses the message as soon as it reads the type, and closes the connection when the message is not there yet.
2. The server sends a zero byte, the numbers N and g, the salt as an octet string, the number B, the PBKDF2 iteration count as BE64 and the options as text. The probed Mac sent the 512-byte RFC 5054 modulus, g = 5, a 32-byte salt, 19417 iterations and the options `mda=SHA-512,replay_detection,conf+int=ChaCha20-Poly1305,kdf=SALTED-SHA512-PBKDF2`, in 1163 bytes. It answers an unknown account name the same way, with a random salt.
3. The client sends the number A, the proof M1 as an octet string, its selected options as text and 16 random bytes as an octet string.
4. The server sends its proof M2 as an octet string, 16 bytes as an octet string, an empty text and a BE32 zero, and then the SecurityResult. When M1 is wrong it sends only a SecurityResult of 1.

The values follow corecrypto's default SRP variant. H is SHA-512. PAD left-pads a number to 512 bytes. The account name selects the verifier on the Mac and enters no hash: the identity in x and in M1 is the empty string.

```
P  = PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512(password, salt, iterations, 128 bytes)
x  = H(salt | H(":" | P))
k  = H(PAD(N) | PAD(g))
u  = H(PAD(A) | PAD(B))
A  = g^a,  B = k g^x + g^b
S  = (B - k g^x)^(a + u x)
K  = H(PAD(S))
M1 = H((H(PAD(N)) xor H(PAD(g))) | H("") | salt | PAD(A) | PAD(B) | K)
M2 = H(PAD(A) | M1 | K)
wrapping key = first 16 bytes of SHA-256(K)
```

The options name a ChaCha20-Poly1305 layer. That layer belongs to the SASL mechanism and is not used on the RFB connection. After the SecurityResult the connection is clear until the record layer starts, as described above.

Type 33 wraps either of the other two logins in RSA. Its messages are `[BE32 length][LE16 1]["RSA1"][BE16 kind][body]`. Kind 0 asks for the server's key, and the server answers with a SubjectPublicKeyInfo. The probed Mac sent a 294-byte RSA-2048 key. Kind 1 carries the 128-byte block of type 30 under AES-128-ECB with a key the viewer chooses and encrypts to the server's RSA key. Kind 2 carries the SRP messages above, with the first one under RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 encryption, and AppleVNCServer accepts it only when it also offered type 36. Nothing authenticates the RSA key. Screen Sharing stores the key under a label, and when the server sends another key it imports that key and retries without asking the user. Kind 1 therefore gives the password to an impersonator that sends its own key. Kind 2 gives the same guarantee as type 36 and hides the account name from passive observers only. Apple mode does not implement type 33: kind 2 would add the RSA envelope for no protection against an impersonator.

`srp.c` is Remora's implementation of type 36 on OpenSSL's big numbers, PBKDF2 and digests. It accepts only the modulus and generator above, a B between 1 and N - 1, a nonzero u, 1 to 2,000,000 PBKDF2 iterations, a challenge of exactly its declared length and options that include the four it selects. The iteration bound keeps a server from stalling the client. Anything else ends the attempt with native error 8 before the client computes a proof. After the client sends M1, a SecurityResult of 1 or 2 is a rejected name or password. Any other answer than the correct M2, compared in constant time, ends the attempt with native error 19 before ClientInit. Account names over 255 bytes are refused locally.

The evidence, by source:

- `passwordserver_sasl-215`, `cyrus_sasl/plugins/srp.c`: the field encodings in `MakeBuffer` and `UnBuffer` (lines 579 to 970, which also reject trailing bytes), the server steps (1786 to 2118), the client steps (2421 to 2795) and `CalculateSALTED_SHA512_PBKDF2` (972).
- [corecrypto](https://github.com/apple/corecrypto), `ccsrp/src`: `ccsrp_ctx_init` selects `CCSRP_OPTION_SRP6a_HASH`, and `ccsrp_generate_x.c`, `ccsrp_generate_K_from_S.c`, `ccsrp_generate_M.c` and `ccsrp_generate_H_AMK.c` give the formulas. corecrypto was read and nothing was copied.
- AppleVNCServer of macOS 27.0.1 (26A434), arm64e, UUID `0B190195-B069-31BD-A275-E2764DD59656`: the dispatch for type `0x24` at `0x100010bb8` calls `SendSRPChallenge` (`0x100042464`) at once. `srp_server_mech_step` (`0x100063e04`) parses the first message with the format `%s%s%s%o` (`0x100063ea4`), reads the account's record from the second text (`0x100064048`), fills a random 32-byte salt for an unknown account (`0x1000643ec`), and parses the answer with `%m%-o%s%-o` (`0x100063f5c`) before `ccsrp_server_compute_session(srp, "", saltlen, salt, A)` (`0x100064650`). On completion `SendSRPChallenge` hashes the session key with `CC_SHA256` (`0x1000429c8`) and passes the first 16 bytes to `SetupAESKeys` (`0x1000429dc`). The refusal of RSA-wrapped SRP without type 36 is at `0x100041b6c`.
- ScreenSharing.framework of the same build, UUID `EC0B2C20-F816-3FCE-822D-F9403C09EB50`: `_RFBAuthenticateCore` writes `[0x24][BE32 length][message]` in one call (`0x1CC13F8C0` to `0x1CC13F8F4`). `_srp_client_mech_step` (`0x1CC13A39C`) builds the first message from `("", name, "", empty)` (`0x1CC13A794`), parses the challenge with `%c%m%m%o%m%q%s` (`0x1CC13A488`), calls `CCKeyDerivationPBKDF` with HMAC-SHA512 for 128 bytes (`0x1CC13AB98`) and `ccsrp_client_process_challenge(srp, "", 128, P, saltlen, salt, B, M1)` (`0x1CC13ABEC`), writes `%m%o%s%o` (`0x1CC13ACB4`), and parses the server's proof with `%-o%-o%s%u` (`0x1CC13A520`) before `ccsrp_client_verify_session` (`0x1CC13A708`). The wrapping key is `CC_SHA256` of the session key (`0x1CC141F68`) into `SetupAESKeys` (`0x1CC141F7C`). For type 33, the key request is built at `0x1CC13F974`, a new key is imported without a prompt at `0x1CC1400C4`, and `SecKeyEncrypt` runs with PKCS#1 padding at `0x1CC136C58`.
- The Mac itself, by probes that sent no proof: the offer list, the type 36 challenge for an account name that does not exist, the closed connection when the type byte and the first message were written separately, and the type 33 key answer. The modulus it sent has SHA-256 `4ee95187682bcb230ad26a95205f6920e84708f6251b3894329b09ec23919e33`, which is also the digest of OpenSSL's `BN_get_rfc3526_prime_4096`.

The arithmetic is checked against Apple's. `../tests/srp_oracle.py` is a loopback peer that computes the verifier, B, the check of M1, M2 and K with the `ccsrp` functions that `/usr/lib/system/libcorecrypto.dylib` exports, called as AppleVNCServer calls them. On macOS 27.0.1 (26A434) the sanitized client completed that login and decoded three frames through records keyed from corecrypto's K. The loopback peer `ard_peer.py` implements the server a second time with Python integers and `hashlib`. Its cases cover a correct login, a wrong password, six offers without type 36, nine unsupported challenges, and a peer without the verifier that answers with a made-up proof or with a bare success result. In the last two the peer receives M1, fails to verify it, and sees the client close without another byte. The answer and the server's proof have not run against a real Mac: no login was attempted from this implementation before it was merged.

## Display selection and protocol evidence

The session lists physical displays from DisplayInfo2 and selects exactly one with SetDisplay (`0x0d`): `[type][combineAll=0][two zero bytes][BE32 display ID]`. There is no combined-display operation in the session API. Startup chooses the remotely flagged main display; if none is flagged, it chooses the first entry ordered by desktop x, y and display ID. Apple entry flag bit 0 identifies the main display. Desktop positions and framebuffer bounds are distinct; the session exposes desktop positions and physical pixel sizes.

DisplayInfo2 arrives as pseudo-encoding 1105 or server message `0x51`. Both carriers have a BE16 body length. The body contains a 20-byte header and 56 bytes per display. The parser accepts 1 through 64 entries, requires the exact declared length, rejects duplicate or reserved IDs, and validates pixel dimensions before allocation. Header pixel width and height determine selected framebuffer geometry, including a switch between equally sized displays. DisplayInfo 1101 is bounded and consumed for compatibility; it does not replace DisplayInfo2's main flag or geometry.

A 2026-11-13 native bridge probe against macOS 26.6.2 verified both Apple 003.889 and standard RFB 3.8. That server emitted DisplayInfo2 only when both 1101 and 1105 were advertised. It reported display 2 as main, 5120x2880 at desktop (0,0), and display 1 as 3024x1964 at (-1512,1440). Each dialect completed main 2 -> display 1 -> display 2 in one connection. Each transition delivered one fully initialized, nonblack picture at 5120x2880, 3024x1964 and 5120x2880, respectively, with native error 0. The probe sent no keyboard or pointer events and changed no remote display settings. Its private numeric receipts remain under `.snap/display-probe/` in the implementation worktree.

The standard Mac path keeps standard authentication and input framing. It requests lossless ZRLE/Raw, sends control SetMode 1, subscribes to AutoFBUpdate, and retries a full non-incremental request once per second while coverage is incomplete. The tested server initially sent only changed subrectangles after some selections; a later full request produced the missing complete picture. Display acknowledgements request a fresh picture and renew the subscription at the selected size. The client does not switch to Apple 003.889 to obtain this behavior. Standard mode retains its existing policy of continuing updates while hidden; Apple mode can pause its subscription.

An admitted switch clears readiness immediately. The worker cancels queued input and receipts, releases held input before SetDisplay, and resets its pointer state. It discards publication of in-flight old pictures. A matching DisplayInfo2 acknowledgement resets pixel and DCT coverage even when the dimensions are unchanged. Pixels reach FrameSink only after every selected pixel is initialized and every rectangle in the message validates. Input remains blocked until that picture is delivered. A switch has a ten-second bound that acknowledgements cannot extend; failure reports `DisplaySelectionFailure.timedOut` and leaves input and captures blocked until a successful retry. If the selected ID disappears, the session selects the remaining main display or deterministic first display. A new connection starts with a fresh inventory and the same startup policy; no display preference is saved.

Ordinary single-framebuffer VNC servers remain supported. Generic multi-display selection through ExtendedDesktopSize is not implemented. An applied ExtendedDesktopSize layout with more than one screen, without Apple display-selection metadata, ends the session with native error 12 before decoding subsequent combined pixel rectangles. A server that never reports its physical layout can only be treated as one framebuffer; Remora cannot discover unreported physical displays. No generic multi-screen selection or combined-display fallback is claimed.

Owned decoder and sanitized adapter tests initialize separate regions, accept partial updates inside initialized regions, and stop partial skips or DCT updates in untouched regions. Adapter tests check that the session then requests the screen in full and draws the full update that answers. Raw coverage tests include partial tiles and same-size picture resets. Public session fixtures cover both metadata carriers, remote-main startup, same-size switches with in-flight old pixels, input release before selection, incomplete-picture timeout and retry, and selection after unplug. These tests do not establish physical hot-unplug behavior on every server release. Physical hot-unplug and live input targeting were not performed during this display-selection probe.

## Responsiveness on LAN

On 2026-11-13, before Apple mode gained session encryption, a development build on a MacBook Pro M4 Pro running macOS 27.0.1 was compared with Screen Sharing's standard connection using Adaptive Quality against a MacBook Pro M3 Pro running macOS 26.6.2 over Ethernet. Both clients showed the same 3024x1964 desktop in a 1512x1034 window. A local probe posted physical input and timed the first changed pixels with ScreenCaptureKit, requesting 120 Hz capture on a 60 Hz display. These are captured-response measurements, not physical display latency.

Six alternating Apple-mode/Screen Sharing pairs ran one client at a time, with 16 trials per action per round. Scroll alternated six lines down and up, typing alternated one A and Delete, and menu trials opened TextEdit's File menu and closed it with Escape. The pointer stayed outside the typing region. All 576 planned inputs produced a response. Each insertion shifted the watched line by one cell and each deletion restored it. Every menu remained open for its planned Escape. Independent host process-log checks found no external native-test activity during any pair. No pair or performed observation was replaced or excluded.

The primary estimate is the median of six round medians. Scroll pools both directions; typing measures insertion and menu measures opening. Gaps are Apple mode minus Screen Sharing, in milliseconds.

| Action | Apple mode | Screen Sharing | Gap | 95% paired-cluster interval for gap |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Scroll | 67.7 | 64.4 | +3.3 | [-1.4, +9.8] |
| Type | 58.3 | 64.1 | -5.8 | [-9.5, -1.7] |
| Open menu | 127.8 | 119.4 | +8.4 | [+6.3, +14.8] |

All three observed primary gaps meet the 10 ms point-estimate rule. The menu interval extends beyond 10 ms, so the experiment does not establish that its gap is within 10 ms with 95% confidence. Pooling all menu trials instead gives a 12.4 ms median gap with interval [9.5, 15.6]; that is a different estimate from the prespecified median of round medians.

Trial-level interquartile ranges and confidence intervals replace the original ordering of six observed round standard deviations, as agreed for this series. Each action/direction cell has 48 observations per client.

| Action/direction | IQR Apple / Screen Sharing | IQR gap | 95% paired-cluster interval |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Scroll down | 10.5 / 13.1 | -2.6 | [-8.7, -0.2] |
| Scroll up | 12.5 / 14.4 | -2.0 | [-8.4, +4.3] |
| Insert | 15.6 / 9.4 | +6.2 | [+1.4, +9.1] |
| Delete | 13.4 / 14.0 | -0.6 | [-6.6, +7.4] |
| Open menu | 6.6 / 12.6 | -6.0 | [-11.3, +1.3] |
| Close menu | 15.2 / 14.4 | +0.8 | [-5.8, +10.6] |

Typing insertion has a wider observed IQR in Remora. The prespecified global one-sided spread test gives 19/64 = 0.2969 by swapping whole paired rounds jointly across all six cells. Non-rejection does not establish equal spread or equivalence. The six-round population standard deviations, reported descriptively as Apple / Screen Sharing, are 2.92 / 2.79 ms for scroll, 3.05 / 2.55 for typing, and 3.19 / 2.43 for opening a menu. Confidence intervals use 20,000 paired-cluster bootstrap draws and only six paired clusters. Fixed client order, drift and the small number of clusters limit their interpretation.

The [numeric observations, method, environment audit and reproducer](../../Tools/vnc/benchmarks/2026-11-13/README.md) contain all 576 observations and the complete analysis. Earlier G, H, J and K runs are retained separately and are not pooled into these results. H stopped after a Screen Sharing menu opened and closed before Escape; its cause remains unknown. J stopped on a missing typed glyph, and K stopped on a menu-opening timeout. Host logs match those two Remora incidents and K's earlier menu closures to unrelated native AppKit tests that created key panels on the served Mac. No trace identifies the exact input hop in either incident. This series used a process-log validity rule fixed before collection and encountered no such test run. It does not establish general input reliability.

A separate prospective control compared Apple mode, standard VNC and Screen Sharing with the same 1200 ms quiet period and 8-second settling deadline. It recorded both first changed pixels and the first frame matching the eventual watched region, ignoring only the fixed blinking-caret box for settling and completion matching. Completion uses sampled luminance differences above 48 and the original frame timestamp; it does not add the quiet period. The first-response search and its three-second deadline stayed unchanged. These single-round controls are descriptive and are not pooled into the six-pair analysis.

The table gives first-change / watched-region-completion medians in milliseconds. Scroll uses both directions; the other rows have eight observations per client, except standard-mode menu rows as noted below.

| Action | Apple first / complete | Screen Sharing first / complete | Standard first / complete |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Scroll | 70.0 / 96.4 | 74.8 / 81.9 | 614.3 / 664.7 |
| Insert | 67.8 / 67.8 | 65.2 / 65.2 | 62.2 / 62.2 |
| Delete | 70.0 / 70.0 | 61.4 / 61.4 | 61.6 / 61.6 |
| Open menu | 127.0 / 127.0 | 122.1 / 135.8 | 1124.3 / 1513.2 |
| Close menu | 100.9 / 170.5 | 105.7 / 170.9 | 130.1 / 314.0 |

Apple mode and Screen Sharing each completed all 48 control inputs. Standard mode completed scroll and typing, then its eighth menu opening exceeded the three-second response search. A later capture showed the open menu. The table's standard-mode menu medians therefore condition on seven observed openings and seven closings; one performed opening timed out and the final planned closing was not attempted. The timeout and stopped round are retained, without replacement or imputation. In this control, Apple mode was faster for scrolling and menus; single-key typing was comparable and does not show an Apple-mode advantage.

An earlier standard-mode attempt with the original 400 ms quiet rule stopped when a partial text repaint failed the restoration guard. A later capture showed the restored text. That attempt remains separate. The longer-quiet control was fixed before collecting any of its three client rounds. [Control observations and method](../../Tools/vnc/benchmarks/2026-11-13/COMPLETION-METHOD.txt) retain both metrics, the timeout, sample counts and source hashes.


The decoder and image-quality settings are unchanged. The 303-second editing workload below ran on `36e595f`; later changes preserve window presentation demand and recover a startup timeout. In the earlier 2026-11-08 comparison, Escape in Preview's empty search field left the focus ring visible in both Remora and Screen Sharing; that behavior came from Preview.

## Connection reliability

On 2026-11-12 a signed development build on macOS 27.0.1 connected to a MacBook Pro M3 Pro running macOS 26.6.2 over LAN. A final run on `a9a3584` completed 100 consecutive Apple-mode connections, each returning a nonblack 3024x1964 picture. Every attempt saved a PNG, independently decoded its pixels and recorded its SHA-256 before closing the session. This run needed no recovery handshake. An earlier build also passed 100 consecutive connections, plus three connections that each followed 180 seconds with no VNC client connected. The host used its existing display policy on AC power. Final receipts and images are under `.snap/benchmark/connects-recovery/`; earlier evidence is under `.snap/benchmark/connects-final/` and `.snap/benchmark/connects-idle/`.

Before the recovery fix, one of 112 authenticated connections to the same host received no ServerInit. The host was awake and unlocked. Remora's summary read `native_error=6 phase=18 last_success=17 failure=10`: ARD authentication succeeded and ClientInit was written, but no ServerInit byte arrived before the 10-second read deadline. The host's log and `screensharingd` disassembly identify a lost wakeup in macOS 26.6.2 (25G83). Its authentication thread wakes the server loop before adding the authenticated socket to the descriptor set. The loop can then wait indefinitely without that socket. In the failed connection the log order was reversed from all 111 successful connections, and the server read the waiting ClientInit only when another client connected 224.7 seconds later. macOS 27.0.1 (26A434) adds the socket before sending the wakeup. Nine other first connections to newly started daemons succeeded, so daemon startup or idle time alone does not explain the stall. Logs, analysis and disassembly extracts are under `.snap/serverinit-timeout/`.

Remora recovers from exactly this state once per session. When the Apple profile's SRP login has succeeded, ClientInit has been written, and the ServerInit read reaches its deadline without receiving a byte, the bridge reports error 11. The session worker then frees that native context, with its socket, decoder state and session key. It opens one new context to the same endpoint with the same profile and the same credentials. A password typed for the first transport is reused for the second and then dropped. Rejected authentication, cancellation, EOF, a partial ServerInit and standard mode are never retried, and no other security type is tried. The existing 20-second connection deadline covers both transports. Each transport writes its own handshake summary under the same attempt UUID, and the first keeps `native_error=11` with its phase and failure numbers. `appleWithheldServerInitRecoversOnceOnAFreshTransport` covers the recovery against the independent loopback peer. The stall cannot be forced on a real host. The one real-host observation is the manual reconnect 224.7 seconds later, which succeeded while the stalled viewer was still registered.

A 303-second TextEdit workload completed 100 paired typing/deleting, scrolling and File-menu cycles with live frames throughout. Periodic PNGs and independently decoded movie frames showed no visible decoding errors. A static first-line region matched the initial capture exactly after the workload, and the generated document's saved bytes were unchanged. Evidence is under `.snap/apple-editing/run-20261112T133657Z-db7fdf/`.

On 2026-11-22 a development build of this branch on the same MacBook Pro M4 Pro connected in Apple mode to the MacBook Pro M3 Pro running macOS 26.6.2 over Ethernet. Apple mode requires the encrypted record layer, so every connection that drew a picture was encrypted. Clipboard text crossed in both directions inside the encrypted session, including 760,000 bytes from the Mac and 494,999 bytes to it with equal SHA-256 digests on both sides. Keyboard input opened and closed the Mac's launcher, and the picture decoded correctly.

In the same setup, 2 of 8 connections ended at startup with "The Apple desktop update could not be decoded." Both times, a 105-byte partial update for the 3024x8 strip at the top of the screen arrived before any full update had covered it. The `main` build at `45f92ae` has the same failure: one of its CPU runs below needed a second connection. With the adapter change described above, 12 of 12 connections stayed up and drew correct pictures.

CPU was then measured on the M4 Pro with `top`, averaging 30 one-second samples of the Remora Dev process while its window showed the session. Two rounds alternated a build of `main` at `45f92ae` with this branch. Updates per second count frame callbacks. The two workloads ran on the M3 Pro: a zoomed Terminal window listing `/usr/bin` in a loop, and a browser window animating 60 circles and 20 lines of text on a gradient at the display's frame rate.

| Workload | `main` CPU | Branch CPU | `main` updates/s | Branch updates/s |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Terminal listing | 2.9%, 6.6% | 4.5%, 3.7% | 8, 19 | 18, 14 |
| Browser animation | 62.6%, 62.2% | 52.1%, 52.2% | 140, 139 | 125, 125 |

Under the animation the branch used 16% less CPU while also decrypting every record. Per update, that is 0.42% against 0.45%. The branch's busiest thread ran at about 49% and was often idle, so the lower update rate came from the Mac, not from Remora. The 82% recorded after #115 used a workload that was not written down, so these runs do not repeat it.
